name: Calculus
description: Authored practice spanning the supplied 24-lecture syllabus: functions, limits, differentiation, integration, sequences, series, complex numbers and multivariable calculus. Problems are independent teaching exercises, not reproduced examination questions.
limitations: Scope follows the supplied local lecture transcription and course overview, not a live 2026-27 syllabus verification. Historical assessment rules are deliberately omitted.

Lecture PDFs are predominantly image-based. Text extraction was attempted for all 24; only representative pages were visually inspected. The supplied Lectures.md transcription is the main content source and contains OCR errors; formulas here were independently reconstructed.
The supplementary formula sheet contains errors, including the complex exponential identity and a geometric-series interval. It is not treated as authoritative.
Notes and selected 2023 examination PDFs were sampled for scope and style; the complete textbook, all examinations, recordings and linked interactive videos were not reviewed.
Source references identify conceptual grounding, not an original exercise number or an official answer key. Every exercise here is newly authored.
Open responses require human self-review against explanations and rubrics and must never be automatically graded. This portable data file has no application integration or grading implementation.

sources.locator: Lectures 1-3: functions, inverse trigonometric functions, continuity, limit definitions, squeeze theorem and asymptotes
Lectures 4-6: linearization, extrema, mean value theorem, implicit differentiation, Newton's method and l'Hospital's rule
Lectures 7-8: fundamental theorem, symmetry, substitution and integration by parts
Lectures 9-10: improper integrals, sequences, fixed points and monotone convergence
Lectures 11-13: geometric and p-series, comparison, alternating series, error bounds and ratio test
Lectures 13-15: power series, endpoints, termwise operations, Taylor polynomials and analytic functions
Lectures 16-17: vectors, domains, level sets, multivariable limits, partial derivatives and tangent planes
Lectures 18-19: chain rule, unit directional derivatives, gradients, critical points and second derivative test
Lectures 20-21: complex arithmetic, polar form, exponentials, roots and polynomial factorization
Lectures 22-23: double integrals over rectangles and type I/type II regions
Learning objectives and lecture schedule; historical course code CSE1200

topics.name: Functions, continuity and limits
topics.description: Control domains and inverse branches before computing local and infinite limits.

skills.name: Domains and inverses
skills.description: Combine domain restrictions and choose valid inverse branches.

skills.name: Limit reasoning
skills.description: Use algebra, one-sided limits, squeeze bounds and asymptotic division.

lesson.title: A formula needs a domain
paragraphs: The domain records where every operation is defined. Square roots require a nonnegative radicand, logarithms a strictly positive argument, and denominators must be nonzero. Intersect these restrictions rather than handling them separately. For sqrt(5-x)/(x-1), the domain is (-infinity,1) union (1,5].

An inverse reverses a one-to-one function on its range. Squaring is not one-to-one on all real numbers: on [0,infinity) its inverse is the nonnegative square root. Likewise arcsin returns angles in [-pi/2,pi/2], so arcsin(sin(5pi/6)) equals pi/6, not 5pi/6.

lesson.title: Limits concern nearby values
paragraphs: A limit may exist where the function is undefined. For (x^2-4)/(x-2), cancellation gives x+2 only when x is not 2, which is enough to prove that the limit at 2 is 4. Defining the missing value as 4 makes the extension continuous.

A two-sided limit requires equal left and right limits. To establish a limit rigorously, start with an arbitrary epsilon>0 and choose a delta so that 0<|x-a|<delta forces |f(x)-L|<epsilon. For f(x)=3x+1 at a=2, delta=epsilon/3 works.

At infinity, divide a rational function by its highest denominator power. For (2x^2+3x+1)/(x+1), polynomial division gives 2x+1 exactly away from -1; for a nonzero remainder tending to zero the quotient line is an oblique asymptote. A cancelled factor usually indicates a hole, whereas a remaining denominator zero can produce a vertical asymptote.

exercises.title: Intersect domain restrictions
exercises.prompt: Find the real domain of sqrt(6-x)/(x-2). Explain each excluded value.
exercises.explanation: The radicand requires x<=6 and the denominator requires x!=2. The domain is (-infinity,2) union (2,6].
rubric: Exclude x=2 and express the intersection.

exercises.title: Invert a restricted quadratic
exercises.prompt: For f(x)=(x-1)^2 with x>=1, find f inverse and its domain.
exercises.explanation: From y=(x-1)^2 and x-1>=0, x=1+sqrt(y). Thus f inverse(y)=1+sqrt(y) for y>=0.

exercises.title: Principal inverse angle
exercises.prompt: Which is arcsin(sin(7pi/6))?
exercises.explanation: sin(7pi/6)=-1/2; the angle in the principal arcsin interval with that sine is -pi/6.

exercises.title: Remove a hole
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as x approaches 3 of (x^2-9)/(x-3).
exercises.explanation: For x!=3 the quotient is x+3, so its limit is 6.

exercises.title: Rationalize a difference
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as x approaches 0 of (sqrt(9+x)-3)/x, showing the rationalization.
exercises.explanation: Multiplying by the conjugate gives 1/(sqrt(9+x)+3) for x!=0. The limit is 1/6.
rubric: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
Obtain and evaluate the nonsingular expression.

exercises.title: Join two branches
exercises.prompt: Let f(x)=2x+a for x<1 and f(x)=x^2+4 for x>=1. Find a so that f is continuous at 1.
exercises.explanation: The left limit is 2+a and the right value is 5. Equating them gives a=3.

exercises.title: Squeeze oscillation
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as x approaches 0 of x sin(1/x), with justification.
exercises.explanation: The absolute value is at most |x|, which tends to zero. The squeeze theorem gives limit 0 even though sin(1/x) alone has no limit.

exercises.title: Find an oblique asymptote
exercises.prompt: Find the oblique asymptote of (x^2+3x+5)/(x+1) and justify it by division.
exercises.explanation: Division gives x+2+3/(x+1). The remainder tends to zero at either infinity, so the line is y=x+2.
rubric: Explain why the remainder tends to zero.

exercises.title: Infinity and square roots
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as x approaches negative infinity of x/sqrt(x^2+4).
exercises.explanation: sqrt(x^2+4)=|x|sqrt(1+4/x^2). For negative x, x/|x|=-1.

exercises.title: Build an epsilon-delta proof
exercises.prompt: Prove from the epsilon-delta definition that lim as x approaches 4 of (5x-2) is 18.
exercises.explanation: Given epsilon>0, choose delta=epsilon/5. If 0<|x-4|<delta, then |(5x-2)-18|=5|x-4|<epsilon.
rubric: Choose a positive delta and establish the required inequality.

topics.name: Derivatives and their applications
topics.description: Differentiate compositions and implicit curves, approximate locally, and check theorem hypotheses.

skills.name: Differentiate and linearize
skills.description: Apply product, chain and implicit differentiation rules.

skills.name: Apply derivative theorems
skills.description: Use extrema tests, Newton iteration, the mean value theorem and l'Hospital's rule.

lesson.title: Local change
paragraphs: The derivative measures the slope of a tangent. Product and chain rules track different sources of change: for x exp(x^2), the derivative is exp(x^2)+2x^2 exp(x^2). For an implicit curve, treat y as y(x); differentiating x^2+xy+y^2=7 gives 2x+y+(x+2y)y'=0.

The linearization at a is L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a). For sqrt(x) near 4 this is 2+(x-4)/4; at 4.04 it predicts 2.01. This is an approximation, not an identity. The differential dy=f'(a)dx describes its predicted change.

lesson.title: Theorems require conditions
paragraphs: For extrema on a closed interval, compare values at endpoints and all interior critical numbers, including places where the derivative does not exist. A zero derivative alone does not prove an extremum: x^3 has a horizontal tangent at zero and keeps increasing.

Newton's update is x_next=x-f(x)/f'(x), the x-intercept of the current tangent line. For f(x)=x^2-5 at x=2 it gives 9/4. The method needs a nonzero derivative at each step and is not guaranteed to converge from every starting point.

The mean value theorem needs continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b). L'Hospital's rule applies to suitable 0/0 or infinity/infinity quotients with differentiability and nonzero denominator derivative near the limit point, provided the derivative quotient has a limit. A product or power must first be rewritten into an eligible quotient; never differentiate numerator and denominator of a regular quotient just to evaluate its limit.

exercises.title: Product and chain together
exercises.prompt: For f(x)=x^2 exp(3x), find f'(x).
exercises.explanation: The product rule gives 2x exp(3x)+3x^2 exp(3x)=exp(3x)(2x+3x^2).

exercises.title: Implicit tangent slope
exercises.prompt: On x^2+xy+y^2=7, compute dy/dx at (1,2).
exercises.explanation: Differentiation gives (x+2y)y'=-(2x+y). At (1,2), y'=-4/5.
rubric: Apply the product rule to xy.
Evaluate the derivative at the stated point.

exercises.title: Tangent intercept
exercises.prompt: Find the y-intercept of the tangent to y=x^3-2x at x=2.
exercises.explanation: The point is (2,4) and slope is 3(2)^2-2=10. Thus y-4=10(x-2), or y=10x-16.

exercises.title: Estimate a logarithm
exercises.prompt: Use the linearization of ln(x) at x=1 to estimate ln(1.03). State whether this overestimates or underestimates the true value.
exercises.explanation: L(x)=x-1, so the estimate is 0.03. Since the second derivative -1/x^2 is negative, the graph is concave down and the tangent overestimates it.
rubric: Justify the error direction using concavity.

exercises.title: Mean value point
exercises.prompt: For f(x)=x^2 on [1,5], find the c in (1,5) supplied by the mean value theorem.
exercises.explanation: The secant slope is (25-1)/4=6. Solving f'(c)=2c=6 gives c=3; the polynomial meets both hypotheses.

exercises.title: One Newton step
exercises.prompt: Apply one Newton step to f(x)=x^2-8 starting from x0=4. Give x1.

exercises.title: Closed-interval extrema
exercises.prompt: Find the absolute minimum and maximum of f(x)=x^3-3x on [-2,2], including all locations where each is attained.
exercises.explanation: The critical numbers are -1 and 1. Values at -2,-1,1,2 are -2,2,-2,2. The minimum -2 occurs at -2 and 1; the maximum 2 occurs at -1 and 2.
rubric: Compare endpoints and critical values and report tied locations.

exercises.title: Eligible derivative quotient
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as x approaches 0 of (exp(4x)-1)/x.
exercises.explanation: This is 0/0; l'Hospital gives the limit of 4exp(4x), namely 4.

exercises.title: Reject an invalid rule application
exercises.prompt: A student replaces lim as x approaches 0 of (1+sin x)/(2+x) by lim cos(x)/1=1. Explain the error and find the correct limit.
exercises.explanation: The quotient approaches 1/2, not an indeterminate form. Direct continuity gives 1/2; l'Hospital's hypotheses do not hold.
rubric: Identify that neither 0/0 nor infinity/infinity occurs.

exercises.title: Logarithm of an indeterminate power
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as x approaches 0 of (1+2x)^(1/x), explaining why logarithms help.
exercises.explanation: Near zero the base is positive. The logarithm is ln(1+2x)/x, a 0/0 quotient whose limit is 2. Exponentiating gives exp(2).
rubric: Take the logarithm of the positive expression.
Evaluate the quotient limit and exponentiate.

topics.name: Definite integrals and techniques
topics.description: Interpret accumulation and select substitution or integration by parts.

skills.name: Accumulation and substitution
skills.description: Use Riemann sums, the fundamental theorem and changes of variable.

skills.name: Integration by parts
skills.description: Choose factors, track boundaries and construct a reduction relation.

lesson.title: Accumulation and substitution
paragraphs: A definite integral is a limit of signed rectangle sums. If f is continuous, an antiderivative F evaluates its accumulation: integral from a to b of f is F(b)-F(a). Differentiating an accumulation with moving upper bound g(x) gives f(g(x))g'(x); a moving lower bound contributes a negative term.

Substitution reverses the chain rule. For integral from 0 to 1 of 2x exp(x^2) dx, let u=x^2, so du=2x dx and the bounds become 0 and 1. The integral is exp(1)-1. Changing bounds keeps the entire calculation in u and prevents mixing variables.

Signed integral and geometric area differ when a graph crosses the axis. The integral of x over [-1,1] is zero by odd symmetry, but the area between the graph and axis is 1. To compute area, split at zeros and integrate the absolute value.

lesson.title: Parts reverses the product rule
paragraphs: The identity integral u dv = uv - integral v du transfers a derivative from one factor to another. For integral x cos(x) dx, choose u=x and dv=cos(x)dx. The result is x sin(x)+cos(x)+C. Differentiation checks the cancellation of the extra sine terms.

For a definite integral, evaluate the boundary product as well as the remaining integral. Repeated parts can reduce a polynomial degree: if I_n=integral from 0 to 1 of x^n exp(x) dx, then for n>=1, I_n=e-n I_(n-1), with I_0=e-1. The initial value matters just as much as the recurrence.

exercises.title: Recognize a Riemann sum
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as n tends to infinity of (1/n) sum from k=1 to n of 6(k/n)^2.
exercises.explanation: This is the right-endpoint Riemann sum for integral from 0 to 1 of 6x^2 dx, which equals 2.

exercises.title: Both endpoints move
exercises.prompt: If F(x)=integral from x to x^2 of (t+1) dt, compute F'(2).

exercises.title: Substitute with bounds
exercises.prompt: Evaluate integral from 0 to 1 of 6x(x^2+1)^2 dx.
exercises.explanation: Set u=x^2+1. The integral becomes 3 times integral from 1 to 2 of u^2 du=[u^3]_1^2=7.

exercises.title: Odd symmetry
exercises.prompt: Evaluate integral from -2 to 2 of x^3 cos(x) dx.
exercises.explanation: x^3 is odd and cos(x) is even, so their product is odd. Its integral over a symmetric interval is zero.

exercises.title: Area rather than signed accumulation
exercises.prompt: Find the area between y=x-1 and the x-axis for 0<=x<=3.
exercises.explanation: Split at x=1. The two triangles have areas 1/2 and 2, giving total area 5/2. The signed integral would instead be 3/2.

exercises.title: Logarithmic substitution
exercises.prompt: Find an antiderivative of 2x/(x^2+5).
exercises.explanation: With u=x^2+5 the integral is ln(u)+C=ln(x^2+5)+C; the argument is always positive.
rubric: Match the numerator to the derivative of the denominator.

exercises.title: Polynomial times exponential
exercises.prompt: Evaluate integral from 0 to 1 of x exp(x) dx.
exercises.explanation: An antiderivative is (x-1)exp(x). Its value at 1 is 0 and at 0 is -1.

exercises.title: Integrate a logarithm
exercises.prompt: Find integral ln(x) dx on x>0, showing the parts choice.
exercises.explanation: Take u=ln(x), dv=dx. Then du=dx/x and v=x, so the integral is x ln(x)-x+C.
rubric: Evaluate the remaining integral and include C.

exercises.title: Parts twice
exercises.prompt: Find an antiderivative of x^2 cos(x).
exercises.explanation: First parts gives x^2 sin(x)-2 integral x sin(x) dx. A second application gives x^2 sin(x)+2x cos(x)-2sin(x)+C.
rubric: Preserve signs and verify by differentiation.

exercises.title: Derive a reduction formula
exercises.prompt: Let J_n=integral from 0 to pi/2 of sin(x)^n dx. Derive J_n=((n-1)/n)J_(n-2) for integers n>=2 and state J_0,J_1.
exercises.explanation: Use u=sin(x)^(n-1), dv=sin(x)dx. The boundary term vanishes and J_n=(n-1) integral sin(x)^(n-2)cos(x)^2 dx=(n-1)(J_(n-2)-J_n). Rearrangement gives the recurrence. J_0=pi/2 and J_1=1.
rubric: Explain the vanishing boundary term for n>=2.

topics.name: Improper integrals and sequences
topics.description: Replace infinite operations with limits and justify recursive convergence.

skills.name: Improper integral convergence
skills.description: Handle infinite endpoints and singularities separately.

skills.name: Sequence convergence
skills.description: Combine bounds, monotonicity, subsequences and fixed-point equations.

lesson.title: Improper means take a limit
paragraphs: For integral from 1 to infinity of x^(-p), first integrate to R, then send R to infinity. It converges exactly when p>1. Near zero the condition reverses: integral from 0 to 1 of x^(-p) converges exactly when p<1. Location of the problematic endpoint matters.

An interior singularity must be split into two independent improper integrals. Symmetric cancellation cannot rescue divergence. For integral from -1 to 1 of 1/x, each half diverges, even though symmetric truncated integrals are zero. That zero is a principal value, not the ordinary improper integral.

lesson.title: A fixed point is only a candidate
paragraphs: A convergent sequence is a list whose tail becomes arbitrarily close to one value. Boundedness alone is insufficient: (-1)^n stays bounded but oscillates. Monotone increasing sequences bounded above, and monotone decreasing sequences bounded below, do converge.

Consider a_0=0 and a_(n+1)=(a_n+6)/2. Induction gives a_n<=6 and a_(n+1)-a_n=(6-a_n)/2>=0. The sequence therefore converges. Only now may continuity be used to solve L=(L+6)/2, giving L=6. Subtracting 6 also yields a_n-6=-6/2^n, an explicit error formula.

For a recurrence involving a square root, first establish an invariant interval and monotonicity. Solving L=f(L) without proving convergence can produce candidates that are never reached or even coexist with oscillation.

exercises.title: Infinite exponential tail
exercises.prompt: Evaluate integral from 0 to infinity of 4exp(-2x) dx.
exercises.explanation: The integral to R is 2-2exp(-2R), which tends to 2.

exercises.title: Integrable endpoint singularity
exercises.prompt: Evaluate integral from 0 to 1 of 1/sqrt(x) dx.
exercises.explanation: Integrating from epsilon to 1 gives 2-2sqrt(epsilon), which tends to 2.

exercises.title: An interior pole
exercises.prompt: Does integral from -1 to 2 of 1/x^2 dx converge? Justify the answer without substituting across zero.
exercises.explanation: Split at zero. Integral from epsilon to 2 equals 1/epsilon-1/2, which diverges; the left half also diverges. The full integral diverges to positive infinity.
rubric: Demonstrate divergence by a one-sided limit.

exercises.title: Comparison at infinity
exercises.prompt: Prove that integral from 1 to infinity of 1/(x^2+sqrt(x)) dx converges.
exercises.explanation: For x>=1 the integrand is nonnegative and at most 1/x^2. The comparison integral converges, so the given integral converges.
rubric: Give a valid upper bound for a nonnegative integrand.

exercises.title: Two endpoint requirements
exercises.prompt: For which real p does integral from 0 to infinity of x^(-p) dx converge?
exercises.explanation: Convergence near zero requires p<1, whereas convergence at infinity requires p>1. Both cannot hold; p=1 diverges at both ends.

exercises.title: A rational sequence
exercises.prompt: Find lim as n tends to infinity of (7n^2-3)/(n^2+2n).
exercises.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by n^2; lower-order terms tend to zero.

exercises.title: Bounded but divergent
exercises.prompt: Explain why a_n=(-1)^n+1/n does not converge, despite being bounded.
exercises.explanation: The even subsequence tends to 1 and the odd subsequence tends to -1. A convergent sequence would force both subsequences to have the same limit.
rubric: Use their different limits to conclude divergence.

exercises.title: Recursive square root
exercises.prompt: Let a_0=0 and a_(n+1)=sqrt(6+a_n). Prove convergence and determine the limit.
exercises.explanation: The interval [0,3] is invariant. On it sqrt(6+a)>=a since 6+a-a^2=(3-a)(a+2)>=0. Thus the sequence increases and is bounded above by 3. Its nonnegative limit satisfies L^2=6+L, so L=3 rather than -2.
rubric: Prove the invariant bound and monotonicity.
Invoke monotone convergence before solving for L.

exercises.title: Find a tail threshold
exercises.prompt: For a_n=5+3/2^n with n>=0, find the smallest integer N such that |a_n-5|<1/10 for every n>=N.
exercises.explanation: We need 2^n>30. Since 2^4=16 and 2^5=32, the first valid index is 5 and the errors decrease afterwards.

exercises.title: Fixed-point trap
exercises.prompt: A student claims x_(n+1)=2-x_n with x_0=0 converges to 1 because L=2-L. Diagnose the argument.
exercises.explanation: The actual terms alternate 0,2,0,2,... and do not converge. The fixed-point equation describes a necessary condition if convergence holds; it does not establish convergence.
rubric: Distinguish a necessary fixed-point condition from a convergence proof.

topics.name: Numerical series and convergence tests
topics.description: Distinguish terms from partial sums, choose a suitable test and bound truncation error.

skills.name: Sum structured series
skills.description: Evaluate geometric and telescoping series.

skills.name: Classify convergence
skills.description: Use term, comparison, alternating, integral and ratio tests with their hypotheses.

lesson.title: Convergence belongs to partial sums
paragraphs: A series converges when its partial sums converge. Its terms must tend to zero, but this condition alone is not enough: the harmonic terms 1/n tend to zero while their sum diverges. A geometric series beginning at n=0 sums to a/(1-r) when |r|<1.

Telescoping means cancellation inside a finite partial sum before a limit is taken. Since 1/[n(n+1)]=1/n-1/(n+1), summing from n=1 to N leaves 1-1/(N+1). Its limit is 1. Writing the finite remainder prevents an unjustified cancellation of infinite expressions.

lesson.title: Choose a test by structure
paragraphs: Positive rational terms often compare with a p-series. For n/(n^3+1), the ratio to 1/n^2 tends to 1, so both converge. The integral test requires an eventually positive, continuous, decreasing function matching the terms. A factorial or exponential often makes the ratio test efficient.

If the absolute successive-term ratio tends to L<1, there is absolute convergence; if L>1, divergence follows. L=1 is inconclusive. For alternating terms (-1)^(n-1)b_n, decreasing nonnegative b_n tending to zero ensure convergence and an error no larger than the first omitted b_n.

Absolute convergence means the series of absolute values converges. Conditional convergence means the original series converges but its absolute-value series diverges. For the alternating harmonic series, the alternating test proves convergence and the harmonic series proves failure of absolute convergence.

exercises.title: Geometric starting index
exercises.prompt: Evaluate sum from n=1 to infinity of 6/2^n.
exercises.explanation: The first term is 3 and ratio is 1/2, so the sum is 3/(1-1/2)=6.

exercises.title: Telescoping with an offset
exercises.prompt: Evaluate sum from n=1 to infinity of 1/((n+1)(n+2)), displaying the finite partial sum.
exercises.explanation: The nth term is 1/(n+1)-1/(n+2). The sum to N is 1/2-1/(N+2), so the infinite sum is 1/2.
rubric: Retain the end term before taking its limit.

exercises.title: Necessary condition first
exercises.prompt: Does sum from n=1 to infinity of (3n+1)/(n+4) converge? Explain the quickest decisive test.
exercises.explanation: Its terms tend to 3, not zero, so the series diverges by the term test.
rubric: Apply the necessary condition for series convergence.

exercises.title: Limit comparison
exercises.prompt: Classify sum from n=1 to infinity of n/(n^3+7), justifying a comparison.
exercises.explanation: The ratio to 1/n^2 is n^3/(n^3+7), tending to 1. The p-series with p=2 converges, so the given positive series converges.
rubric: Compute a positive finite ratio limit.

exercises.title: Conditional or absolute
exercises.prompt: Classify sum from n=1 to infinity of (-1)^(n-1)/sqrt(n).
exercises.explanation: The magnitudes decrease to zero, so the alternating series converges. Their sum is a divergent p-series with p=1/2.

exercises.title: Guaranteed alternating accuracy
exercises.prompt: Using the alternating-series bound, what is the smallest N guaranteeing that the first N terms of sum from n=1 to infinity of (-1)^(n-1)/n^2 have error at most 1/100?
exercises.explanation: The bound is 1/(N+1)^2. Requiring it to be <=1/100 gives N+1>=10, hence N=9. This is the smallest N certified by this bound.

exercises.title: Factorial in the denominator
exercises.prompt: Use the ratio test on sum from n=0 to infinity of 5^n/n!.
exercises.explanation: The successive-term ratio is 5/(n+1), tending to zero. The series converges absolutely.

exercises.title: Inconclusive ratio
exercises.prompt: The ratio test gives L=1 for sum 1/n and sum 1/n^2. What does this imply?

options.text: The ratio test decides neither; use another test

exercises.explanation: L=1 is inconclusive. The p-series test then distinguishes the divergent harmonic series from the convergent p=2 series.

exercises.title: Logarithmic integral test
exercises.prompt: Determine convergence of sum from n=2 to infinity of 1/(n(ln n)^2).
exercises.explanation: f(x)=1/(x(ln x)^2) is positive, continuous and decreasing for x>=2. With u=ln x, its integral to infinity is 1/ln 2, finite. The series converges by the integral test.
rubric: Use logarithmic substitution and a finite improper integral.

exercises.title: A shrinking term is insufficient
exercises.prompt: Give a positive decreasing sequence a_n tending to zero whose series diverges, and justify divergence.
exercises.explanation: Take a_n=1/n. It decreases to zero, but integral from 1 to R of 1/x dx=ln R tends to infinity, so the integral test proves divergence.
rubric: Give a sequence meeting all three term conditions.
Prove series divergence rather than merely assert it.

topics.name: Power series and Taylor approximation
topics.description: Track centers, convergence intervals, coefficients and approximation error.

skills.name: Power-series operations
skills.description: Determine radius and endpoints and differentiate or integrate inside the radius.

skills.name: Taylor polynomials
skills.description: Construct local polynomial approximations and bound their remainder.

lesson.title: Radius is not the whole interval
paragraphs: A power series sum c_n(x-a)^n is centered at a. A ratio test typically gives |x-a|<R for absolute convergence. Each endpoint must then be tested separately; convergence at one endpoint says nothing about the other.

For sum x^n/n from n=1, R=1. At x=1 it is harmonic and diverges; at x=-1 it is alternating harmonic and converges. Its interval is [-1,1). Within the open interval, integrating the geometric series gives -ln(1-x)=sum x^n/n. Endpoint validity needs its own reasoning.
Termwise differentiation and integration preserve the radius of a power series, but can change endpoint convergence. Substituting x^2 into 1/(1-x)=sum x^n gives 1/(1-x^2)=sum x^(2n) for |x|<1.

lesson.title: Taylor coefficients record derivatives
paragraphs: The degree-m Taylor polynomial at a is sum from n=0 to m of f^(n)(a)(x-a)^n/n!. For exp(x) at zero, the cubic polynomial is 1+x+x^2/2+x^3/6. The coefficient of x^3 is 1/6, while the third derivative at zero is 1.

If |f^(m+1)(t)|<=M between a and x, Taylor's theorem bounds the error by M|x-a|^(m+1)/(m+1)!. A Taylor series equals a function only where its remainder tends to zero; being infinitely differentiable alone does not guarantee equality. Standard exponential and trigonometric series do converge to their functions everywhere.

exercises.title: A shifted radius
exercises.prompt: Find the radius of convergence of sum from n=1 to infinity of (x-2)^n/(n 4^n).
exercises.explanation: The absolute successive-term ratio tends to |x-2|/4, so the radius is 4.

exercises.title: Both endpoints
exercises.prompt: Find the full convergence interval of sum from n=1 to infinity of (x-1)^n/(n 2^n).
exercises.explanation: The radius is 2 around 1. At x=-1 the alternating harmonic series converges; at x=3 the harmonic series diverges. The interval is [-1,3).

exercises.title: Geometric substitution
exercises.prompt: Write the Maclaurin series of 1/(1+3x), including its open convergence interval.
exercises.explanation: Substitute -3x into the geometric series: sum from n=0 to infinity of (-3)^n x^n, valid for |x|<1/3.
rubric: Include the constant term and alternating coefficients.

exercises.title: Differentiate a known series
exercises.prompt: Evaluate sum from n=1 to infinity of n/2^(n-1).
exercises.explanation: Differentiating sum x^n=1/(1-x) inside |x|<1 yields sum n x^(n-1)=1/(1-x)^2. Set x=1/2.

exercises.title: Integrate to obtain a logarithm
exercises.prompt: Derive a power series for ln(1+x) by integrating 1/(1+x) from 0 to x. State validity for |x|<1.
exercises.explanation: Inside |t|<1, 1/(1+t)=sum from n=0 of (-1)^n t^n. Termwise integration gives sum from n=1 of (-1)^(n-1)x^n/n. The lower bound sets the constant to zero.
rubric: Integrate each term and shift the index correctly.
State the open interval and integration constant condition.

exercises.title: Coefficient extraction
exercises.prompt: What is the coefficient of x^4 in the Maclaurin series of exp(2x)? Give an exact fraction.
exercises.explanation: The x^4 coefficient is 2^4/4!=16/24=2/3.
rubric: Use the factorial in the Taylor coefficient.

exercises.title: Derivative from a series
exercises.explanation: The x^6 coefficient in 1+x^2+x^4+x^6+... is 1, so f^(6)(0)=6!=720.

exercises.title: Expansion away from zero
exercises.prompt: Find the degree-two Taylor polynomial of ln(x) about x=2.
exercises.explanation: The value, first derivative and second derivative at 2 are ln 2, 1/2 and -1/4. Thus T_2(x)=ln 2+(x-2)/2-(x-2)^2/8.

exercises.title: A justified sine approximation
exercises.prompt: Approximate sin(0.2) with its cubic Maclaurin polynomial and give an alternating-series error bound.
exercises.explanation: The approximation is 0.2-0.2^3/6=149/750, approximately 0.1986667. The next omitted magnitude is 0.2^5/120=1/375000, and the subsequent magnitudes decrease, so the absolute error is at most that number.
rubric: Bound the error with the x^5/120 term.

exercises.title: Series resolves cancellation
exercises.prompt: Evaluate lim as x approaches 0 of (cos(2x)-1)/x^2.
exercises.explanation: cos(2x)=1-2x^2+O(x^4). After subtracting 1 and dividing by x^2 the limit is -2.

topics.name: Multivariable functions and partial derivatives
topics.description: Read domains and level sets, test limits, and build tangent-plane approximations.

skills.name: Geometry and limits
skills.description: Interpret vectors, level curves, domains and approach paths.

skills.name: Partials and tangent planes
skills.description: Differentiate one coordinate at a time and assemble the total linear approximation.

lesson.title: More than one direction of approach
paragraphs: A function f(x,y) assigns a height to each allowed point in the plane. For ln(9-x^2-y^2), the domain is the open disk x^2+y^2<9. Level sets f(x,y)=c join points of equal height; x^2+4y^2=c gives ellipses for c>0.

A multivariable limit must agree along every path. For xy/(x^2+y^2), the x-axis gives zero and y=x gives 1/2, proving that no limit exists at the origin. Agreement on two paths cannot prove existence; a bound controlling all paths can.
The dot product u dot v=sum u_i v_i relates lengths and angles through u dot v=||u||||v||cos(theta). For (1,2) and (2,-1) it is zero, so the two nonzero vectors are perpendicular.

lesson.title: Partial changes combine into a plane
paragraphs: A partial derivative holds other independent variables fixed. For f=x^2 y+sin(y), f_x=2xy and f_y=x^2+cos(y). Mixed partials agree when the relevant second partial derivatives are continuous in a neighborhood, as they are here.

For differentiable f, L(x,y)=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b). For x^2+xy at (1,2), the value is 3 and partials are 4 and 1, giving L=3+4(x-1)+(y-2). This predicts the change under simultaneous small shifts in both coordinates.

Existence of two partial derivatives at a point alone is not enough for differentiability. A convenient sufficient condition is continuity of the first partials near the point. Differentiability guarantees that the linearization error divided by the distance to the point tends to zero.

exercises.title: A multivariable logarithm domain
exercises.prompt: Describe the real domain of ln(4-x^2-y^2), including whether the boundary belongs.
exercises.explanation: The argument must be strictly positive, so x^2+y^2<4. This is the open disk of radius 2 centered at the origin; its boundary is excluded.
rubric: Identify the disk and boundary exclusion.

exercises.title: Read a contour
exercises.prompt: Describe the level set f(x,y)=9 for f(x,y)=x^2+9y^2 and give its axis intercepts.
exercises.explanation: The level set is x^2/9+y^2=1, an ellipse. Its intercepts are (3,0),(-3,0),(0,1),(0,-1).

exercises.title: Dot product geometry
exercises.explanation: Multiply corresponding entries and add: 2-4+6=4.

exercises.title: Disprove a two-variable limit
exercises.prompt: Show that x^2/(x^2+y^2) has no limit at (0,0).
exercises.explanation: Along y=0 with x!=0 the value is 1. Along x=0 with y!=0 it is 0. The distinct path limits rule out a common limit.

exercises.title: Prove a limit with a bound
exercises.prompt: Prove that x^2 y/(x^2+y^2) tends to zero as (x,y) tends to (0,0).
exercises.explanation: Away from the origin, |x^2 y/(x^2+y^2)|<=|y|<=sqrt(x^2+y^2). The last quantity tends to zero, giving the limit by squeezing.
rubric: Use a bound valid for every approach direction.
Conclude using distance to the origin.

exercises.title: Partial evaluation
exercises.prompt: For f(x,y)=x^2 y+3y^2, find f_x(2,3).
exercises.explanation: Holding y fixed gives f_x=2xy; at (2,3) this is 12.

exercises.title: Mixed partials
exercises.prompt: For f(x,y)=x^2 y^3, compute f_xy(1,2).
exercises.explanation: f_x=2xy^3 and f_xy=6xy^2; evaluation gives 24.

exercises.title: Tangent plane
exercises.prompt: Find the tangent plane to z=x^2+2y^2 at the graph point above (1,-1).
exercises.explanation: The graph point is (1,-1,3), with f_x=2 and f_y=-4 there. The plane is z=3+2(x-1)-4(y+1), equivalently z=2x-4y-3.
rubric: Compute the graph height and both partials.
Anchor the plane at the correct point.

exercises.title: Total differential
exercises.prompt: Use the total differential of f(x,y)=xy at (2,3) to estimate the change when dx=0.1 and dy=-0.2.
exercises.explanation: df=y dx+x dy=3(0.1)+2(-0.2)=-0.1. The actual change has the additional product dx dy=-0.02, so it is -0.12.
rubric: Report the estimate as -0.1, not an exact equality for the finite change.

exercises.title: When can mixed partials be exchanged?
exercises.prompt: Which hypothesis guarantees f_xy(a,b)=f_yx(a,b)?

options.text: Both mixed partial derivatives are continuous in a neighborhood of (a,b)

exercises.explanation: Clairaut's theorem gives equality under continuity of the mixed second partials in a neighborhood. The weaker statements do not suffice.

topics.name: Gradients, chain rule and extrema
topics.description: Follow changes along curves, normalize directions and classify critical points.

skills.name: Directional change
skills.description: Combine gradients with velocities or unit direction vectors.

skills.name: Multivariable optimization
skills.description: Use the Hessian discriminant and inspect boundaries for global extrema.

lesson.title: Gradient and motion
paragraphs: For z=f(x(t),y(t)), the chain rule is dz/dt=f_x x'(t)+f_y y'(t). The velocity is allowed to have any length. In contrast, the directional derivative D_u f=gradient(f) dot u is conventionally defined using a unit direction u.

For f=x^2+3y at (1,2), the gradient is (2,3). In the direction (3,4), normalize to (3/5,4/5); the directional derivative is 18/5. Its maximum over unit directions is sqrt(13), attained along (2,3)/sqrt(13). At a noncritical point the gradient is perpendicular to the level curve.

lesson.title: Critical points and boundaries
paragraphs: Interior extrema of a differentiable function must have zero gradient. At a critical point of a twice continuously differentiable function, let D=f_xx f_yy-f_xy^2. If D>0, the sign of f_xx distinguishes a minimum from a maximum. D<0 gives a saddle, and D=0 is inconclusive.

For x^2+xy+y^2, the only critical point is the origin. The Hessian entries are 2,1,2, giving D=3>0 and a strict minimum. For x^2-y^2, D=-4 and the origin is a saddle: one axis increases the function and the other decreases it.

A continuous function on a closed bounded region attains global extrema, but they may occur on its boundary. For x+y on the unit square, the gradient never vanishes; evaluating the boundary gives minimum 0 at (0,0) and maximum 2 at (1,1). Reduce each boundary piece to a one-variable problem and include corners.

exercises.title: Chain rule along a curve
exercises.prompt: Let f(x,y)=x^2+y^2, x(t)=t and y(t)=t^2. Find d/dt f(x(t),y(t)) at t=1.
exercises.explanation: The chain rule gives 2x(1)+2y(2t)=2t+4t^3, equal to 6 at t=1.

exercises.title: Normalize the direction
exercises.prompt: For f(x,y)=3x+4y, find the directional derivative in the direction of (6,8).
exercises.explanation: The unit direction is (3/5,4/5). Dotting it with the gradient (3,4) gives 9/5+16/5=5.

exercises.title: Steepest increase
exercises.prompt: At a point where gradient f=(-3,4), give the unit direction of steepest ascent and the maximum directional derivative.
exercises.explanation: The gradient norm is 5. The unit ascent direction is (-3/5,4/5), and the maximum derivative is 5 by the dot-product bound.
rubric: Give its norm as the maximum rate.

exercises.title: Tangent to a level curve
exercises.prompt: Find a tangent-line equation to x^2+2y^2=6 at (2,1).
exercises.explanation: The gradient (2x,4y) at (2,1) is (4,4), a normal. Hence 4(x-2)+4(y-1)=0, or x+y=3.
rubric: Evaluate the gradient at the point.
Use it as a normal rather than a tangent direction.

exercises.title: Nested two-variable chain rule
exercises.prompt: Let z=x^2 y, x=u+v and y=u-v. Compute partial z/partial u at (u,v)=(2,1).
exercises.explanation: z_u=(2xy)x_u+x^2 y_u=2xy+x^2. At x=3,y=1 this is 6+9=15.

exercises.title: Classify a quadratic critical point
exercises.prompt: Classify the critical point of f(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2.
exercises.explanation: Solving 2x+y=0 and x+2y=0 gives (0,0). D=2*2-1=3>0 and f_xx=2>0, so it is a strict local minimum, also global by positive definiteness.
rubric: Apply the second derivative test with its sign conditions.

exercises.title: Saddle point
exercises.prompt: Classify the origin for f(x,y)=x^2-4y^2.
exercises.explanation: D=2*(-8)-0=-16<0. Values are positive along the x-axis and negative along the y-axis near the origin.

exercises.title: An inconclusive Hessian
exercises.prompt: At the origin, the second derivative test for f(x,y)=x^4+y^4 gives D=0. Classify the point by another argument.
exercises.explanation: Both fourth powers are nonnegative and their sum is zero only at the origin. Thus the origin is a strict global minimum despite the inconclusive Hessian test.
rubric: Do not infer a saddle from D=0.

exercises.title: Optimize on a rectangle
exercises.prompt: Find the maximum value of f(x,y)=2x-y on 0<=x<=3 and -1<=y<=2.
exercises.explanation: The function increases with x and decreases with y, so the maximum occurs at (3,-1) and equals 7.

exercises.title: Boundary and interior compete
exercises.prompt: Find the absolute extrema of f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x on the closed disk x^2+y^2<=4.
exercises.explanation: Write f=(x-1)^2+y^2-1. The minimum is -1 at the interior point (1,0). On the boundary f=4-2x; it is largest at x=-2,y=0, giving 8. Boundary values and the only interior critical point exhaust candidates.

topics.name: Complex numbers and roots
topics.description: Move between Cartesian, polar and exponential forms while tracking all roots.

skills.name: Complex arithmetic
skills.description: Use conjugates, moduli and correct arguments.

skills.name: Powers and roots
skills.description: Apply Euler's formula and enumerate distinct polynomial roots.

lesson.title: Two coordinates, one number
paragraphs: A complex number z=a+bi has i^2=-1, conjugate a-bi and modulus sqrt(a^2+b^2). Multiplying z by its conjugate gives |z|^2, which turns division into real-denominator arithmetic. For (2+i)/(1-i), multiply by (1+i)/(1+i) to obtain (1+3i)/2.
For z!=0, write z=r(cos(theta)+i sin(theta))=r exp(i theta), where r=|z|. Arguments differ by multiples of 2pi. Use the quadrant as well as the tangent ratio: -1+i has argument 3pi/4, not -pi/4.

lesson.title: Powers multiply angles; roots divide them
paragraphs: Euler's formula exp(i theta)=cos(theta)+i sin(theta) turns multiplication into addition of arguments. De Moivre gives [r exp(i theta)]^n=r^n exp(in theta). Also exp(a+bi)=exp(a)(cos b+i sin b); it is a product, not a sum of exponentials.

If w=r exp(i theta) is nonzero, its nth roots are r^(1/n) exp(i(theta+2pi k)/n), with k=0,...,n-1. These are n equally spaced points on a circle. For z^3=8, the roots have modulus 2 and arguments 0,2pi/3,4pi/3, namely 2,-1+i sqrt(3),-1-i sqrt(3).

A degree-n complex polynomial has n roots counted with multiplicity. For real coefficients, nonreal roots occur in conjugate pairs. Keep multiplicity distinct from the number of different roots: (z-1)^3 has degree 3 but one distinct root.

exercises.title: Product in Cartesian form
exercises.prompt: Compute (2+3i)(1-2i) in Cartesian form.
exercises.explanation: Expansion gives 2-4i+3i-6i^2=8-i.

exercises.title: Divide by a complex number
exercises.prompt: Simplify (3+i)/(1-i).
exercises.explanation: Multiply by (1+i)/(1+i). The numerator is 2+4i and denominator is 2, giving 1+2i.

exercises.title: Modulus
exercises.prompt: Find the modulus of -5+12i.
exercises.explanation: The modulus is sqrt(25+144)=13.

exercises.title: Choose the correct quadrant
exercises.prompt: Give the polar form of -sqrt(3)+i using an argument in [0,2pi).
exercises.explanation: The modulus is 2. The point is in quadrant II with argument 5pi/6, so z=2exp(5pi i/6).

exercises.title: A power via angles
exercises.prompt: Compute the real part of (1+i)^8.
exercises.explanation: 1+i=sqrt(2)exp(i pi/4). The eighth power is 16exp(2pi i)=16.

exercises.title: A complex exponential
exercises.prompt: Express exp(ln(3)+i pi/2) in Cartesian form.
exercises.explanation: exp(ln 3)exp(i pi/2)=3(0+i)=3i.
rubric: Separate into a product of exponentials.
Evaluate sine and cosine at pi/2.

exercises.title: All fourth roots
exercises.prompt: Find all solutions of z^4=16.
exercises.explanation: The roots have modulus 2 and arguments k pi/2 for k=0,1,2,3. They are 2,2i,-2,-2i.
rubric: Explain the modulus and angle pattern.

exercises.title: A quadratic without real roots
exercises.prompt: Solve z^2-4z+13=0 over the complex numbers.
exercises.explanation: Completing the square yields (z-2)^2=-9, hence z=2+3i or 2-3i.
rubric: Handle the negative discriminant or completed square.

exercises.title: Conjugate-root consequence
exercises.prompt: A polynomial with real coefficients has root 2-i. Which other root must it have?
exercises.explanation: Complex conjugation commutes with evaluation of a polynomial with real coefficients. Conjugating p(2-i)=0 yields p(2+i)=0.

exercises.title: Roots and multiplicity
exercises.prompt: For p(z)=(z-1)^2(z^2+1), state the degree, all distinct roots and each multiplicity.
exercises.explanation: The degree is 4. Root 1 has multiplicity 2, while i and -i each have multiplicity 1. The multiplicities total 4 although there are only three distinct roots.
rubric: Factor the quadratic over the complex numbers.
Separate degree, distinct-root count and multiplicities.

topics.name: Double integrals and general regions
topics.description: Build bounds from geometry, change order and interpret area and average value.

skills.name: Rectangular integration
skills.description: Evaluate iterated integrals and use separability or symmetry.

skills.name: Region descriptions
skills.description: Translate type I/type II regions and reverse integration order.

lesson.title: Integrate one coordinate at a time
paragraphs: A double integral accumulates height times small area. For a continuous function on a rectangle, iterated integration may be performed in either order. In the inner integral, the other coordinate behaves as a constant. On [0,1] x [0,2], integral integral (x+y) dA is integral from 0 to 1 of (2x+2) dx=3.

A product g(x)h(y) separates into two one-variable integrals only when the region is a product of intervals. For xy on [0,2] x [0,3], the integral is (integral x dx)(integral y dy)=2*(9/2)=9. Variable boundaries usually prevent this factorization.

lesson.title: Bounds describe the region
paragraphs: A type I region has a<=x<=b and g_1(x)<=y<=g_2(x). Its integral is integral_a^b integral_g1(x)^g2(x) f dy dx. For the triangle 0<=y<=x<=1, reversing the order gives 0<=y<=1 and y<=x<=1, so the new integral is integral_0^1 integral_y^1 f dx dy.

Reversing order can make an otherwise awkward integral elementary. For integral from 0 to 1 in x and x to 1 in y of exp(y^2), the reversed inner integral is over 0<=x<=y. It contributes a factor y, leaving integral_0^1 y exp(y^2)dy=(e-1)/2.

The integral of 1 is area. The average of f over a region of positive finite area is its double integral divided by that area. If a region must be split to describe slices correctly, integrate each piece and add; a diagram or explicit inequalities should justify every bound.

exercises.title: Rectangle accumulation
exercises.prompt: Evaluate the double integral of x+y over [0,2] x [0,1].
exercises.explanation: Integrating in y gives x+1/2. Its integral from x=0 to 2 is 2+1=3.

exercises.title: Product on a rectangle
exercises.prompt: Evaluate the double integral of 6xy over [0,1] x [0,2].
exercises.explanation: Separability gives 6*(integral_0^1 x dx)*(integral_0^2 y dy)=6*(1/2)*2=6.

exercises.title: Symmetry in one coordinate
exercises.prompt: Evaluate the double integral of x exp(y) over [-2,2] x [0,1].
exercises.explanation: For every fixed y, the inner integral of the odd function x exp(y) over [-2,2] is zero.

exercises.title: Average height
exercises.prompt: Find the average value of f(x,y)=x+2y on [0,2] x [0,2].
exercises.explanation: The integral is 12 and the area is 4, so the average is 3. Equivalently the coordinate averages are both 1.

exercises.title: Triangle area from bounds
exercises.prompt: Evaluate integral from x=0 to 2 of integral from y=0 to x of 1 dy dx.
exercises.explanation: The inner integral is x and integral_0^2 x dx=2, the triangle's area.

exercises.title: Reverse a triangle
exercises.prompt: Reverse the integration order for integral from x=0 to 2 of integral from y=0 to 2-x of f(x,y) dy dx, for continuous f.
exercises.explanation: The region is x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=2. Thus 0<=y<=2 and 0<=x<=2-y. The reversed integral is integral_0^2 integral_0^(2-y) f(x,y) dx dy.
rubric: State the same triangle as inequalities.
Change the order and both bounds consistently.

exercises.title: Curved lower boundary
exercises.prompt: Find the area between y=x^2 and y=x for 0<=x<=1 using a double integral.
exercises.explanation: The region has x^2<=y<=x. Its area is integral_0^1 integral_(x^2)^x 1 dy dx=integral_0^1 (x-x^2)dx=1/6.
rubric: Identify which curve lies above the other.

exercises.title: Change order to find an antiderivative
exercises.prompt: Evaluate integral from x=0 to 1 of integral from y=x to 1 of exp(y^2) dy dx by changing order.
exercises.explanation: The reversed bounds are 0<=y<=1,0<=x<=y. Integrating in x leaves integral_0^1 y exp(y^2)dy=(e-1)/2.
rubric: Integrate out x, then substitute u=y^2.

exercises.title: Reverse a region between curves
exercises.prompt: Describe the region 0<=x<=1, x^2<=y<=x with y as the outer variable.
exercises.explanation: Here 0<=y<=1. The inequalities become x>=y and x<=sqrt(y), so y<=x<=sqrt(y). The positive root is selected because x>=0.
rubric: Select the nonnegative square root and order the x bounds.

exercises.title: Weighted triangular region
exercises.prompt: Evaluate the double integral of 3x over the triangle x>=0, y>=0, x+y<=2.
exercises.explanation: Integrate 3x over 0<=y<=2-x, then x from 0 to 2: integral_0^2 (6x-3x^2)dx=[3x^2-x^3]_0^2=4.
